title: Seward Buys Alaska
text:
After the Crimean War, Russia saw its colony in North America, Russian America, as a burden. It was far from St. Petersburg, made little money, and would be almost impossible to defend against Britain, whose Canadian territory lay next door. Russia preferred to sell it to the United States rather than see it fall to the British.

In March 1867 the Russian minister in Washington, Eduard de Stoeckl, opened talks with Secretary of State William Seward, a keen believer in American expansion. They worked quickly, and the treaty was signed in the early hours of 30 March 1867. The price was 7.2 million dollars, roughly two cents an acre, for about 586,000 square miles.

The purchase drew mockery from some newspapers and politicians, who called Alaska Seward's Folly or Seward's Icebox and asked what anyone would do with a land of ice. But the Senate approved the treaty by a large majority, helped by the influential senator Charles Sumner, and in October 1867 the American flag was raised at Sitka.

The doubters were proved wrong. Gold was found in the region in the 1880s and 1890s, the fisheries and timber were rich, and in 1968 huge oil reserves were discovered at Prudhoe Bay. Alaska's strategic position also became important in the Second World War and the Cold War. It became a state in 1959.
lesson: Some opportunities look foolish at the time because their value lies far in the future. Judge a long-term purchase by what it could become, not by its current use.
people: William Seward, Eduard de Stoeckl, Charles Sumner, Alexander II
source: Treaty concerning the Cession of the Russian Possessions in North America (1867); contemporary press
caveat: Historians note that the press mockery was less widespread than legend suggests, since many newspapers supported the purchase.
